Desirous
dē-zīr´ŭs
adj. (wishing for; eager after — used in Scripture of good longings and of ruinous ones alike)
Old French desirous, from Latin desiderare, to long for. The word is morally neutral in itself; Scripture judges it entirely by its object, and sets the objects side by side.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Proverbs warns of the wrong object: “Be not desirous of his dainties: for they are deceitful meat” (Pro 23:3). Herod wanted a spectacle: “he was desirous to see him of a long season… and he hoped to have seen some miracle done by him” (Luk 23:8). A governor wanted an arrest: “the governor under Aretas the king kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desirous to apprehend me” (2Co 11:32). The disciples wanted an explanation, and Christ met them in it: “Now Jesus knew that they were desirous to ask him” (Joh 16:19). Paul names the deadly form: “Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another” (Gal 5:26).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines desirous as wishing for, coveting, solicitous to possess and enjoy; and desire as an emotion directed to the obtaining or enjoyment of an object.

expand to see more

DESIROUS, a. Wishing for; coveting; solicitous to possess and enjoy.

DESIRE, n. An emotion or excitement of the mind, directed to the attainment or possession of an object from which pleasure is expected.

COVET, v.t. To desire inordinately; to desire that which it is unlawful to obtain or possess.

Key Scripture

Pro 23:3 — "Be not desirous of his dainties: for they are deceitful meat."

Luk 23:8 — "And when Herod saw Jesus, he was exceeding glad: for he was desirous to see him of a long season, because he had heard many things of him; and he hoped to have seen some miracle done by him."

Joh 16:19 — "Now Jesus knew that they were desirous to ask him, and said unto them, Do ye enquire among yourselves of that I said, A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me?"

Gal 5:26 — "Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another."

Modern Corruption

Herod had wanted to see Christ for a long season and got exactly what he wanted, and Christ answered him nothing.

expand to see more

Luke 23:8 is one of the most chilling verses in the Gospels because the desire in it looks so harmless. Herod had heard many things of Him and was exceeding glad to see Him at last — and what he hoped for was a miracle, a performance, an interesting afternoon. He questioned Him in many words; but He answered him nothing. This is the only person in the Gospels to whom Christ says absolutely nothing. Curiosity about Christ is not the same thing as coming to Him, and the difference is not slight; Herod had already beheaded the Baptist and would shortly mock the Son of God in a gorgeous robe.

The corruption to name is the treatment of Christ as a subject of interest, which is the settled posture of a great deal of religious culture and nearly all of academic religion. It can be sincere, sustained, even affectionate, and it never repents. The Reformed distinction between historical faith and saving faith is aimed at exactly this: devils believe and tremble, Herod was glad, Agrippa was almost persuaded. Paul's warning in Galatians shows the same disease inside the church, where a desire for vain glory turns brethren into rivals. Desire is not the problem; the object is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek thelo (G2309), to will, wish, desire; kenodoxos (G2755), desirous of vain glory; Hebrew avah (H183), to crave, long after.

expand to see more

Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, desire; John 16:19, Luke 23:8.

Greek kenodoxos (G2755) — desirous of vain glory; Galatians 5:26 only.

Hebrew avah (H183) — to desire, crave; Proverbs 23:3, 23:6, Numbers 11:4.

Greek epithumia (G1939) — desire, lust, longing; Galatians 5:16, Philippians 1:23.

Greek epithumeo (G1937) — to desire earnestly; Luke 22:15, 1 Timothy 3:1.

Usage

"“He was desirous to see him of a long season” — and Christ answered him nothing."

"“Be not desirous of his dainties: for they are deceitful meat.”"

"“Let us not be desirous of vain glory” — the church's form of the disease."
